front_blocks.md: What reagents are added to test for carbonate ions, and what observation confirms a positive result?

back_blocks.md: **Dilute acid** is added to the sample, then the gas produced is bubbled through **limewater**.
A positive result is confirmed when the limewater turns **milky (cloudy)**, showing **carbon dioxide** has been produced.

front_blocks.md: To test for halide ions, the sample is first acidified with dilute **..........** acid, then aqueous **..........** nitrate is added.

back_blocks.md: To test for halide ions, the sample is first acidified with dilute **nitric** acid, then aqueous **silver** nitrate is added.

front_blocks.md: What reagents are used to test for nitrate ions, and what observation confirms a positive result?

back_blocks.md: Aqueous **sodium hydroxide** and **aluminium foil** are added to the sample, which is then warmed carefully.
A positive result is confirmed when **ammonia gas** is produced, turning damp red litmus paper **blue**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Chloride, bromide and iodide ions all produce a white precipitate when silver nitrate solution is added.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Chloride gives a **white** precipitate, bromide gives a **cream** precipitate and iodide gives a **yellow** precipitate.

front_blocks.md: Why must hydrochloric acid not be used in the acidification step of the halide ion test?

back_blocks.md: Hydrochloric acid must not be used because it contains **chloride ions**, which would react with **silver nitrate** to form a **white precipitate** and interfere with the results.

front_blocks.md: To test for sulfate ions, the sample is acidified with dilute nitric acid and aqueous **..........** nitrate is added. A **..........** precipitate of barium sulfate confirms the presence of SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>.

back_blocks.md: To test for sulfate ions, the sample is acidified with dilute nitric acid and aqueous **barium** nitrate is added. A **white** precipitate of barium sulfate confirms the presence of SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>.

front_blocks.md: Why must nitric acid be added before barium nitrate in the sulfate ion test?

back_blocks.md: Nitric acid is added first to remove any **carbonate ions** that may be present. Carbonates would also form a **precipitate** with **barium nitrate**, which would interfere with the results.

front_blocks.md: Define **anion**.

back_blocks.md: An **anion** is a negatively charged ion formed when an atom or group of atoms gains one or more electrons.
Non-metal ions such as Cl⁻, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub>⁻ are all examples of anions.

front_blocks.md: How do you test for ammonium ions (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) in solution?

back_blocks.md: Add aqueous sodium hydroxide solution and warm gently. A positive result is confirmed when **ammonia gas** is released, turning **damp red litmus paper blue**.

front_blocks.md: Adding a few drops of sodium hydroxide to Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions produces a **..........** blue precipitate, which is **..........** in excess sodium hydroxide.

back_blocks.md: Adding a few drops of sodium hydroxide to Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions produces a **light** blue precipitate, which is **insoluble** in excess sodium hydroxide.

front_blocks.md: What colour precipitate forms when sodium hydroxide or ammonia solution is added to iron(II) ions, and what happens to this precipitate on standing?

back_blocks.md: A **green precipitate** forms with iron(II) ions (Fe<sup>2+</sup>).
On standing, the precipitate **turns brown** near the surface as the iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Both calcium ions and zinc ions form a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide, but they can be distinguished because the zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

back_blocks.md: **True.**

Both Ca<sup>2+</sup> and Zn<sup>2+</sup> form white precipitates with sodium hydroxide, but the zinc hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution, while the calcium hydroxide precipitate does not dissolve.

front_blocks.md: Why must a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame be used when carrying out a flame test?

back_blocks.md: A blue Bunsen flame must be used because a **yellow (safety) flame** would mask the colour produced by the metal ion, making it impossible to identify the cation accurately.

front_blocks.md: What result is observed when excess aqueous ammonia is added to a solution containing copper(II) ions?

back_blocks.md: When excess aqueous ammonia is added to Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions, the initial light blue precipitate dissolves to form a **dark blue solution**.

front_blocks.md: In a flame test, lithium produces a **..........** flame, potassium produces a **..........** flame and copper produces a **..........** flame.

back_blocks.md: In a flame test, lithium produces a **red** flame, potassium produces a **lilac** flame and copper produces a **blue-green** flame.

front_blocks.md: What colour precipitate is formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) ions?

back_blocks.md: A **red-brown precipitate** is formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) ions (Fe<sup>3+</sup>). This precipitate is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide.

front_blocks.md: What test is used to identify hydrogen gas, and what observation confirms a positive result?

back_blocks.md: A lighted splint is held at the mouth of the test tube.
A positive result is confirmed by a loud **squeaky pop** sound as the hydrogen burns rapidly with oxygen.

A glowing splint is used to test for hydrogen gas.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A lighted (burning) splint is used to test for hydrogen, producing a squeaky pop. A glowing splint is used to test for oxygen, which relights the splint.

front_blocks.md: Why is extinguishing a burning splint not a reliable test for carbon dioxide?

back_blocks.md: Extinguishing a burning splint is not reliable because other gases, such as nitrogen, will also put out a flame.
The definitive test for carbon dioxide is that it turns **limewater milky**.

front_blocks.md: What two observations are seen when chlorine gas is tested with damp litmus paper?

back_blocks.md: Damp blue litmus paper first **turns red** (as chlorine dissolves in water to form an acidic solution) and then **bleaches to white**. The bleaching is the key confirming observation.
